title: Bayo
passages:
The low dock was the Kettle's front step: a hundred meters of pontoon lashed out of plastic drums and truck tire, planked over with doors somebody had unscrewed from the drowned city, riding so low the sea came up between the boards and stayed there until the next swell shoved it out. Wren walked it with the paper log buttoned inside her jacket and the reader's shears in her hip pocket, knocking her thigh every third step like somebody politely asking to be let in. In the other pocket, the twin spool — wire thin as fishing line, with a hand-snipped span in it eleven seconds long. In her fist, a receiver the size of a soap bar, tuned to her spit can, the hard-shell drop-box a diver cuts loose so the boat keeps his record when he doesn't surface. Still pinging. Forty-two meters, six hours of battery, two of them gone.

Behind her the storm bell struck eleven off the arcology, flat bronze with the whole weather behind it, and every man on the dock looked up and then went back to work faster.

The bell-tender was at the mooring ring near the end, sitting on an upturned crate with three hundred meters of wet hawser coiled round his boots and no coat, just a wool sweater gone black at the shoulders. He was working an eye splice — unlaying the rope's three strands and tucking them back into themselves so the line finishes in a loop instead of a knot, every tuck whipped with a turn of orange twine so a man can count them by feel in the dark. Six orange knots done. He was starting a seventh while the first six were still wet.

"Bayo Adisa," Wren said.

He didn't look up. His hands went on tucking. "That's the bell-tender," he said. "I'm the bell-tender." Which wasn't a denial and wasn't an answer, and he said it the way a man says a thing he's said many times to many people.

Ten meters on, two kids had a handline over the side, arguing about whether a fish you can't see counts. Out at the east mole a crane on the power barge swung a crate of somebody's diesel in a slow arc, and the whole dock tilted and knocked when it set down.

"I need a pilot for the Stair," Wren said. "Not a promise. A pilot. The Marrow's got one tide, one bell, and a diver going gray on the deck mat."

"Everybody's got a tide." Tuck. Tuck. He tamped the orange down with his thumbnail.

"Nine minutes ago the warden put his name in her book." Wren took out the log and held it open so the wind could do what it liked with the pages. "Ink. His own hand. And the rig that fixes his lungs is chained to a barge that leaves when that bell hits ten. I've got four hours of can left and one tide, and I've been up and down this dock twice asking. You're the only one who didn't laugh."

"I didn't laugh," Bayo said.

"You didn't look up either."

His hands stopped. Just a beat. Then the tucking started again, and she watched him reach for the marlinspike — the tapered steel spike you pry strands apart with — and pick up a yellow plastic fid instead, and keep working with the wrong tool anyway.

The bell did not strike again. It hung on eleven with the count still running, and eleven was one better than ten, and one better than ten was all the mercy anybody was getting this week.

Four hours, Wren thought. Forty-two meters, four hours, and a voice down there that knew her name and used her voice to say it. She put the receiver in her pocket with the spool and did not put her hand near the shears.

Behind her the Marrow sat against the tire fenders with her deck lit and her boom up, and the bunkroom hatch banged back on its dogs, and Ivo Salas came up out of it into the wind with fifteen minutes of impact-wrench air on his back.

The tank hissed at his shoulder. Salas stopped three paces behind Wren and looked past her at Bayo.

Wren turned. "You're the bell-tender."

Bayo looked up from his rope. His hands were orange-stained to the second knuckle. "I am when somebody needs a bell rung. When they need a pilot through the Stair, I'm Bayo Adisa, and my price is two things."

"Name them."

"One: I keep my berth above the waterline. Not a promise from Sol. From you. I sign it now or I don't cast off." He reached for his fid, missed, picked up the yellow plastic fid again by habit, and set it down. "Two: Ivo Salas never sees my face. Not once. Not while we're on the water, not after. He stays below or he stays behind."

Wren glanced at Salas. The old diver stood with his weight on one leg, watching them with pale eyes. Fourteen months in an air pocket had left him washed out, or maybe it was the depth. "That's a steep price."

"The Stair's a steep place." Bayo stood up, unwinding a length of hawser from around his boots. "It's a flooded service channel under the old arcology foundations. The tide runs it one way, then the other, and there's a rope strung through the towers from before the seas took the city. You ride the tide down the rope and ride it back up when it turns. No motors. No lights. You miss the slack, the water holds you. You let go of the rope, the tide takes you past the Line and you don't remember your mother's name when you surface."

"That's the Line," Salas said quietly. "The depth where the dark starts eating memory. Forty meters, give or take."

Wren didn't look at him. "And if I say no?"

"Then you find another pilot." Bayo coiled the line over his forearm. "There isn't one. The Marrow sits here until the bell shuts the channel, and Dey's lungs fill up on the deck mat while you argue with me. I can get you through. I'm the only one who knows where the rope ends."

Salas shifted his weight. The impact-wrench tank gave a wet exhale. "I can stay below," he said. "I don't need to see the bell-tender's face."

"You need air," Bayo said. "You've got fifteen minutes on that back. The Stair takes longer than that if the tide's against us."

"I said I'd stay below."

"You said a lot of things in an air pocket," Bayo said. His voice had an edge now. "Fifteen minutes, Salas. That's all you've got. Make it count."

He looked at Wren. "So. My berth. Salas below decks. And you don't tell him my name until we're through the Stair. Say yes, and I'll have the Marrow rigged before the bell hits ten."

Wren looked at the receiver in her pocket. Four hours on the spit can. Forty-two meters. A voice that used her voice to say her name.

"Say yes," Bayo said.

The storm bell began its count. One deep bronze note, then another, measuring the minutes left before the channel shut.

It was Salas who moved first. He stepped back to the Marrow's rail and let it carry some of his weight — the way a man does when standing has quietly started to cost him — and from there he looked the wet length of the dock at Bayo Adisa.

Wren watched him do it. She had rebuilt two men from their slates, and she knew the face of a diver reaching for another face: the little frown, the eyes going wide and then narrow, the mouth getting ready to shape a name. She waited for it.

It didn't come.

Salas's face stayed pleasant and empty. His pale eyes went over the bell-tender and filed him as ordinary — a young man on a crate, orange to the knuckle, a sweater gone black at the shoulders. The kind of face a man forgets while he's still looking at it. The old diver tilted his head, and Wren watched him do the thing he must have done a hundred times a day since the pocket: reach for something, and close his hand on the smooth place where it should have been.

"You slide right off me," Salas said. Not unkind. Curious, the way a man is curious about weather. "When a face slides like that, it means the water took it. There's no name under there for me to reach, because there's nothing left to reach with." He rubbed his thumb across two fingers, checking for a coin he already knew he'd spent. "So whatever you're braced for, son, you can put it down."

That landed. Wren saw it land.

Because Bayo had gone still on his crate, and he was braced — the whole of him wound tight, shoulders up, breath held, fourteen months of him leaned into the second when Salas's face would change and know him and say the thing out loud in front of the whole dock. He had spent all that time making sure this exact moment never came.

It had come. And it was harmless. Salas felt nothing at all — no face, no name, no fear — and Bayo's body didn't know that yet, wouldn't take it on a stranger's word.

His hands went back to the rope to have somewhere to be. He picked up the strand for the seventh tuck, laid it into the lay, whipped the orange down hard with his thumbnail, tamped it — and then did the whole thing again. Same strand. Same tuck. The seventh knot tied twice, the second riding crooked on the first, and he didn't seem to feel his own hands doing it. A man who could count orange turns by feel in the pitch dark had lost count with Wren standing over him.

Behind them the bell struck. One flat bronze note, nearer ten now, and out at the east mole the crane swung its diesel crate around and set it down, and the whole dock knocked and tilted under them.

Wren looked at the doubled knot. Then at Bayo's face, which was still smooth, still easy, still promising that nothing had happened. Then back at his hands, which were telling the truth he wouldn't.

"You've gone and tied that one twice," she said.

Bayo looked down at the rope like it belonged to somebody else.

Wren stepped into his space and took his wrist. The rope was wet, and so were his hands. She hauled him around the corner of the bell housing, out of the wind and out of sight of the Marrow's rail. Concrete smelled of old diesel and harbor rot. She let go, but kept her body between him and the dock.

"You tied that knot twice," she said.

"Rope's slick," Bayo said. He wouldn't look at her. His thumb rubbed the orange twine.

"You stopped when Salas spoke. You picked up the yellow fid instead of the marlinspike. You don't make mistakes with your hands, Bayo. You count orange turns by feel in the dark. So why did your hands forget the second he said my diver's name?"

Bayo's jaw tightened. "He's not your diver."

"He's on my boat." Wren rested her hand on the shears in her hip pocket. Not touching them yet. Just letting him feel the weight of them. "You cut his line clean. That's what a clean cut looks like. One pass, no fray. You know what that means on a slate? It means somebody wanted him down there."

"I didn't—"

"Don't lie to me." Wren's voice went low. "I rebuild dead hours for a living. I know when a record's been trimmed. You filed the report. You wrote him off as lost. Say it."

The bell struck. One bronze note, close now. The count was single digits.

Bayo closed his eyes. When he opened them, he was looking at her shoulder, not her face. "Fourteen months ago. I cut his ascent line. Clean. Then I signed the sheet that called him lost. That's it."

"You erased him," Wren said.

"I cut a line on a pocket that was leaking," Bayo said. "The tide was turning. We had to cut everybody loose or lose the whole team. I cut him. I reported him. I went home and slept."

"And now he's standing on my rail with fifteen minutes of air and no memory of your face, because you took it from him twice."

"I didn't take his memory," Bayo said. "The depth did that. I just made sure nobody came looking."

Wren let go of the shears. Her hand was shaking, so she put it in her pocket and balled it into a fist. "You cost him fourteen months. You cost me a pilot who can look his crew in the eye."

Bayo's hands opened on the wet hawser. He didn't answer.

From the Marrow rail, Salas was still looking down at them, pale and empty, his impact-wrench tank hissing at his shoulder. The bell struck again. Six minutes to ten. The channel would shut after that.

Wren looked at Bayo. "Can you still pilot the Stair, or did you cut that rope too?"

Bayo said nothing. The seventh knot stayed crooked between his boots.

Wren waited him out. Rebuilding slates had taught her that a man with something in his record fills a silence before an honest one can be bothered to.

Bayo filled it. "I can pilot it," he said. "I know that channel better than I know this dock. Where the rope's gone soft, where the tide turns mean and where it turns kind. I've run it blind. I've run it in a flat calm with my eyes shut and both hands on the line." A breath. "I didn't cut the Stair. I cut Salas."

"Then here's how it goes." Wren hooked her thumb toward the Marrow — deck lit, boom up, Dey gray under a blanket on the mat. "Bell hits ten, channel shuts, and I am not standing on this dock arguing with a man who won't look at me. We leave with you or we leave without you. With you, we ride the rope clean. Without you, I put the girl at the wheel with the paper log on her knee and we go in ugly, and maybe the tide spits us out the far mouth and maybe it holds us down there long enough that Sol forgets my name and I forget we ever had one worth keeping." She let it sit. "I'd rather go with the one man alive who knows where the rope ends."

Bayo's jaw worked. Out at the east mole the crane swung another crate and set it down, and the dock knocked and tilted, and he swayed with it without thinking, a man whose feet had done this ten thousand times.

"Salas stays below," he said. "That's the second thing and it doesn't move. I'll take your boat through. I'll get your gray diver to the rig and your crates through the gate. But the old man goes under the hatch and stays there till we're out the far side. He doesn't come topside. He doesn't see my face. You put him below and keep him there, and I'm your pilot."

"He'll go below. He's got fifteen minutes of air and a whole pocket's worth of reasons not to fight me on it." Wren didn't move. "But you don't get to make me lie to him about why. I'm done cutting records, Bayo. You want a man hidden, you hide him and you carry what it costs."

"Fine," Bayo said, too quick. "Fine. Below. It's done." And he smiled — a good smile, warm, the kind that had probably talked a dozen crews onto his rope and off a ledge with it. "You'll have the Marrow rigged before the bell. I'll cast off the Stair line myself. Get your people moving. I'll be right behind you."

Wren looked at him.

He hadn't stood up. He was still on the crate, hands back in the wet hawser, laying the strand into the lay for the eighth tuck, whipping the orange down, tamping it with his thumbnail. Tucking. Not rising. A man who'd promised to rig the boat himself and hadn't shifted his weight off the box.

Behind her the bell struck. One flat note. Four minutes, near enough. The sea came up between the dock boards and stayed there.

"You're not moving," Wren said.

"I'll be along." Tuck. Tuck.

"You said you'd rig the line yourself."

"And I will." His eyes stayed on the rope, on the crooked seventh knot, on anything that wasn't the far end of the dock. "Give me a minute. There's always slack water." Slack water — the dead turn when the tide stops to think. There wasn't. Not this tide, not today.

Wren had four hours on a can forty-two meters down, a diver going gray on her deck, and the one man who could get them through the channel had just promised her the moon in a warm voice and sat down to tie the same knot a third time, buying with orange twine the one minute he didn't have before the man he'd cut loose came looking for him.

Salas pushed off the Marrow’s rail and crossed the gangplank to the dock. His impact-wrench tank — a steel cylinder on his back that runs the gun that spins nuts off rusted bolts — hissed at each step. He stopped in front of Bayo’s crate, close enough that Bayo had to crane his neck to look up.

“What’s your name?” Salas said. His voice was soft, the voice of a man who has spent fourteen months talking to the inside of an air pocket and has forgotten how loud the world is.

Bayo’s hands stopped on the orange twine. The fid lay forgotten on the crate. He looked at Salas — really looked — and Wren saw the calculation run through him: say the name and give Salas a handle, or say nothing and break the deal before it’s made.

“Bayo Adisa,” Bayo said.

Salas let the name sit. He turned it over like a stone found in a pocket. “Bayo,” he said. “I don’t know you.”

“No,” Bayo said. “You don’t.”

Wren stepped closer, her hand still near the shears. “He’s the bell-tender. He’s the only pilot who knows the Stair.”

Salas looked at her, then back at Bayo. His pale eyes were empty, but not unkind. “I cut a lot of lines,” he said. “Or I signed the sheets for a lot of them. Does that make me your pilot?”

“It makes you the man who owes me an answer,” Bayo said. His voice had gone smooth again, the warm salesman’s voice, but Wren saw his fingers working the rope underneath, twisting the orange twine until it snapped. “I told you my terms. Salas below. My berth signed. Then I cast off.”

“The bell hits ten in three minutes,” Wren said. “The channel shuts after that. You don’t cast off, you don’t sail.”

“I cast off,” Bayo said. He stood up finally, shaking the wet rope out over his boots. “I just needed to see if he’d remember me.”

Salas tilted his head. “Remember you what?”

“That I cut his line,” Bayo said flatly. “That I signed him lost. That I’m the reason he spent fourteen months in a pocket at forty-two meters.”

Salas blinked. Then he smiled — a small, tired thing. “The depth takes names,” he said. “It takes faces. It takes the reason you were down there. I don’t remember my own brother’s face half the time. Why would I remember yours?”

He looked past Bayo at Wren. “You want me below decks? I’ll go below. I’ve got thirteen minutes of air on this tank, and then I’m just a man in a wet sweater on a dock.” He patted the impact-wrench tank at his shoulder. “Fifteen minutes was the topside promise. It’s down to thirteen.”

The bell struck. One bronze note. Two minutes to ten.

Behind them, on the Marrow’s deck, Dey gave one long, wet cough that didn’t clear anything. He lay still under the blanket, gray as the sky, his mouth slightly open.

Bayo looked at Wren. “He stays below. I take the helm. We go before the bell or we don’t go at all.”

Wren looked at Salas. The old diver stood with his weight on one leg, waiting. His tank gave a wet exhale and then fell silent. The gauge — the round dial that shows how much air is left — dropped to the red.

“You’re out,” Wren said.

“Almost,” Salas said. “But I can still walk.”

“Then walk,” Bayo said. He started toward the Marrow’s gangplank, rope over his shoulder, not looking back at Salas. “Below decks. Stay there till we’re through the Stair. That was the deal.”

Salas followed him. Wren fell in beside Bayo, keeping her body between him and the dock’s edge. “You told him your name,” she said.

“I did.”

“And he doesn’t know you.”

“He doesn’t.”

“Then why were you shaking when you said it?”

Bayo didn’t answer. He stepped onto the Marrow’s deck and turned to help Salas down into the bunkroom hatch. The bell struck again. One minute to ten.

Out at the east mole, the power barge’s engine changed pitch — the deep thrum that means the lung rig is powering up, the machine that washes salt and fluid out of a diver’s lungs. Dey needed that rig. Dey needed it before the bell hit ten.

Wren looked at her receiver in her pocket. Four hours on the can. Forty-two meters. Then she looked at Bayo, who was guiding Salas into the dark below decks with hands that weren’t shaking anymore.

The bell struck. Ten. The channel shut.

And from the Marrow’s rail, Dey’s hand came up from under the blanket, not waving, just reaching for air that wasn’t there.
